history.part3.sub: 2006–today. GPUs, datasets, frameworks and matrix engines.
history.gauss.title: Gauss's Remarkable Theorem
history.gauss.alt: Carl Friedrich Gauss, portrait by Christian Albrecht Jensen, 1840
history.gauss.p1: In 1827 Carl Friedrich Gauss, who was also leading the land survey of the Kingdom of Hanover, presented his "Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas" in Göttingen. Its **Theorema Egregium**, the "remarkable theorem", says that the curvature $K$ of a surface can be computed from lengths measured inside the surface alone, from the coefficients of $ds^2 = E\,du^2 + 2F\,du\,dv + G\,dv^2$, without ever looking at the space around it.
history.gauss.p2: An ant that never leaves its sphere can still find out that the sphere is curved. And no map of the Earth can be both flat and true to scale, because bending a surface leaves $K$ unchanged while flattening a sphere would not. Here the central idea of the tensor first appears: geometry is a small table of numbers at every point, and what matters is what stays the same when the coordinates change.
history.riemann.title: Riemann's lecture: geometry in n dimensions
history.riemann.p1: On 10 June 1854 Bernhard Riemann gave his Habilitation lecture in Göttingen, "Über die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grunde liegen" (On the hypotheses which lie at the foundations of geometry). He had proposed three topics; by custom the first would be chosen, but the 77-year-old Gauss picked the third, the foundations of geometry, and Riemann had to prepare it.
history.riemann.p2: The lecture has almost no formulas, yet it lays out the whole programme: a space of any number $n$ of dimensions whose geometry is fixed by a line element that may change from point to point, in today's notation $ds^2 = g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$, and a curvature that measures how far it is from flat. According to Dedekind, Gauss left deeply impressed. The curvature tensor itself appears in Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay; in $n$ dimensions it has $n^2(n^2-1)/12$ independent components, 1 for a surface and 20 for spacetime. The lecture was printed only in 1868, two years after Riemann's death.
history.christoffel.title: Christoffel's symbols
history.christoffel.alt: Elwin Bruno Christoffel, portrait from the ETH Library
history.christoffel.p1: When the coefficients $g_{ij}$ change from point to point, the ordinary derivative of a vector field depends on the coordinates you happen to use. In 1869 Elwin Bruno Christoffel, until that year a professor at the Zurich Polytechnikum, asked when two quadratic differential forms can be transformed into each other, and in Crelle's Journal introduced the three-index symbols now named after him: $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \tfrac12 g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl} + \partial_j g_{il} - \partial_l g_{ij})$.
history.christoffel.p2: They are not a tensor themselves; they are exactly the correction that turns a derivative into a covariant one. From them Christoffel built a four-index expression equivalent to Riemann's curvature, and his rule for deriving new invariants from old ones is what Ricci would later call covariant differentiation. In 1912 Grossmann would point Einstein to this very paper.
history.ricci.title: Ricci's absolute differential calculus
history.ricci.p1: In Padua, Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro spent roughly 1884 to 1894 turning these ideas into a system, set out in papers between 1888 and 1892. He called it the absolute differential calculus: absolute because its results do not depend on the coordinates. Upper (contravariant) and lower (covariant) indices record how a quantity transforms, contracting an upper with a lower index gives something coordinate-free, and the covariant derivative $\nabla_k$ carries those rules through differentiation.
history.ricci.p2: It was the whole toolbox of tensors, without the word "tensor". For years it found few users: many geometers preferred pictures to pages of indices, and the style was later mocked as "index gymnastics". Élie Cartan is often said to have complained of "débauches d'indices" (a debauch of indices), though no exact source for the phrase is known. As the MacTutor biography puts it, the importance of Ricci's work was not fully understood when he produced it.
history.methodes.title: Ricci and Levi-Civita: the "Méthodes"
history.methodes.alt: Felix Klein, who asked for the 1900 paper
history.methodes.p1: In Göttingen Felix Klein wanted an account of the method that the wider mathematical world would read, and around 1895 he asked Ricci for one. It appeared in 1900 in Mathematische Annalen, volume 54, written with Ricci's former student Tullio Levi-Civita: "Méthodes de calcul différentiel absolu et leurs applications", 77 pages applying the calculus to geometry, mechanics and mathematical physics.
history.methodes.p2: For more than a decade few physicists opened it. Then a Zurich mathematician, looking for the right tool for a friend, would find it. Part I ends here: the mathematics of curved spaces of any dimension is ready, waiting for a physical problem that needs it.
history.voigt.title: Voigt names the tensor
history.voigt.p1: The word came from physics, not geometry. In his 1898 book on the fundamental physical properties of crystals, the Göttingen physicist Woldemar Voigt used "tensor" in roughly today's sense, for the quantities of elasticity, stress and strain, which describe how a material is pulled (Latin tendere, to stretch) differently in different directions. William Rowan Hamilton had used the word in 1846 for something else: the length of a quaternion.
history.voigt.p2: The idea of stress as a table of numbers is older still. In the 1820s Augustin-Louis Cauchy described it for continuous media with nine numbers $\sigma_{ij}$, so that the force per unit area on any face with unit normal $n$ is $t_j = \sigma_{ij} n_i$. Voigt gave the family its name, and it stuck when Einstein and Grossmann used it in 1913 for the objects of the absolute differential calculus.
history.minkowski.title: Minkowski: space and time become one
history.minkowski.alt: Hermann Minkowski, frontispiece of "Raum und Zeit" (1909)
history.minkowski.p1:
On 21 September 1908 in Cologne, Hermann Minkowski opened his lecture "Raum und Zeit" with (in translation): "Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality." Earlier that year he had rewritten electrodynamics in four dimensions: the electric and magnetic fields become one antisymmetric object, today's field tensor $F_{\mu
u}$, and Maxwell's equations shrink to $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u} = \mu_0 J^
u$ and $\partial_{[\lambda} F_{\mu
u]} = 0$.
history.minkowski.p2: Einstein, once his student at the ETH, was at first unimpressed; he is reported to have called the four-dimensional rewriting "superfluous learnedness" (überflüssige Gelehrsamkeit). Within four years he would need far more of it than Minkowski had offered. Minkowski did not see it: he died suddenly in January 1909, aged 44.
history.grossmann.title: "Grossmann, you must help me"
history.grossmann.p1: Einstein's principle of equivalence (1907) said that gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart locally. By the summer of 1912 he had realised that gravity must be described by a variable metric $g_{\mu\nu}$, but he did not know the mathematics of such metrics. In August 1912 he returned to Zurich as professor at the ETH, where his old classmate Marcel Grossmann, whose lecture notes had once carried him through exams, was now professor of geometry.
history.grossmann.p2: As their colleague Louis Kollros recalled four decades later, Einstein pleaded: "Grossmann, Du musst mir helfen, sonst werd' ich verrückt!" (Grossmann, you must help me, or I'll go mad). It is a recollection, not a verbatim record. Grossmann searched the literature and found that the tools already existed: Christoffel, Ricci and Levi-Civita. On 29 October 1912 Einstein wrote to Sommerfeld that he had gained great respect for mathematics, "whose more subtle parts I considered until now, in my ignorance, as pure luxury".
history.entwurf.title: The "Entwurf": a near miss
history.entwurf.alt: Albert Einstein in 1912, photograph by Jan F. Langhans
history.entwurf.p1: In 1913 Einstein and Grossmann published "Entwurf einer verallgemeinerten Relativitätstheorie und einer Theorie der Gravitation" (Outline of a generalised theory of relativity and of a theory of gravitation). Einstein wrote the physical part, Grossmann the mathematical one. For the first time gravity was a metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ with ten independent components, and matter entered through the energy–momentum tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$.
history.entwurf.p2: Einstein's research notebook of 1912–13, the "Zurich Notebook", shows that they examined field equations built from the Ricci tensor, very close to the final answer, and set them aside because they seemed not to give back Newton's law for weak fields and to clash with energy conservation. The Entwurf equations were therefore not generally covariant, and Einstein even devised the "hole argument" to convince himself that this was unavoidable. It cost him two years.
history.levicivita.title: Levi-Civita checks Einstein's mathematics
history.levicivita.p1: In the spring of 1915 Tullio Levi-Civita in Padua read Einstein's 1914 exposition of the Entwurf theory and wrote to say that a key step, Einstein's argument about the covariance of his gravitational equations, was wrong. The letters went back and forth between Padua and Berlin for weeks until Einstein conceded the error. By the autumn he had found further faults in the Entwurf equations and abandoned them.
history.levicivita.p2: In 1917 Levi-Civita gave the covariant derivative a geometric picture: parallel transport, the rule for carrying a vector along a curve in a curved space. That summer Einstein wrote to him, in an often-quoted letter, that it must be nice to ride through these fields "upon the horse of true mathematics" while people like himself had to make their way laboriously on foot (in translation; the English wordings vary).
history.field.title: November 1915: the field equations
history.field.alt: Albert Einstein lecturing in Vienna, 1921, photograph by Ferdinand Schmutzer
history.field.p1:
In November 1915 Einstein presented four papers to the Prussian Academy in Berlin in four weeks. On 18 November he showed that the new theory explains the 43 arcseconds per century of Mercury's perihelion advance that Newton's gravity could not; on 25 November he gave the final, generally covariant field equations. In today's form, $G_{\mu
u} = R_{\mu
u} - 	frac12 R\, g_{\mu
u} =  rac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu
u}$, or $G_{\mu
u} = 8\pi T_{\mu
u}$ in units with $G = c = 1$. David Hilbert reached the same equations from a variational principle at almost the same time.
history.field.p2: Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve, as John Wheeler later summed it up. In his 1916 review "Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie" Einstein also introduced a shorthand: an index that appears twice is summed, and the $\sum$ is no longer written. Every `einsum` still obeys this Einstein summation convention.
history.cuda.title: CUDA: a bet on programmable GPUs
history.cuda.alt: Board of a GeForce 8800 GTX, the first CUDA-capable GPU (2006)
history.cuda.p1: In November 2006 NVIDIA launched the GeForce 8800 GTX, its first GPU built from a unified array of programmable cores, and announced CUDA, a way to program them in C instead of disguising computations as graphics. The toolkit became public in 2007. Every GeForce sold, even to gamers who never used it, carried the extra hardware, so a lab could run matrix multiplications on a games card.
history.cuda.p2: It was an expensive bet. Jensen Huang later recalled that CUDA raised the company's costs by about 50% at a time when its gross margin was around 35%. In the 2008 crisis, on top of a large charge for defective laptop chips, NVIDIA's share price fell by more than 80% from its 2007 peak and the company reported losses, and investors questioned the spending for years. But the popular line that CUDA nearly bankrupted NVIDIA is an exaggeration: its real brush with failure came in 1996–97, before its first hit chip.
history.imagenet.title: ImageNet: data at the scale of the world
history.imagenet.alt: Fei-Fei Li speaking at AI for Good, 2017
history.imagenet.p1: Around 2007 Fei-Fei Li, then a young professor at Princeton, bet that what computer vision lacked was not cleverer algorithms but data. With Kai Li, the student Jia Deng and others she set out to illustrate the nouns of the WordNet hierarchy with hundreds of images each. Labelling by students would have taken decades, so the team turned to Amazon Mechanical Turk: between 2008 and 2010 almost 50,000 workers in 167 countries sorted the candidate images.
history.imagenet.p2: The first paper, at CVPR 2009, described 3.2 million images; the full ImageNet grew to about 14 million images in some 22,000 categories. As Li recounts in her memoir "The Worlds I See", grant applications were turned down and colleagues warned it was a risky use of a young career. From 2010 the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge used a 1,000-class subset with about 1.2 million training images: the benchmark that would make deep learning impossible to ignore.
history.alexnet.title: AlexNet: two gaming GPUs
history.alexnet.alt: A GeForce GTX 580 card with its cooler removed
history.alexnet.p1: Alex Krizhevsky, a PhD student of Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto, wrote cuda-convnet, his own CUDA code for convolutional networks, and with Ilya Sutskever trained an eight-layer network (60 million parameters, 650,000 neurons) on two GeForce GTX 580 cards with 3 GB each, splitting the network between them. Training took five to six days, by Hinton's later telling on a computer in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house.
history.alexnet.p2: At ILSVRC 2012 it reached a top-5 error of 15.3%; the next best entry had 26.2%. Every layer was a tensor operation: convolutions, ReLUs and matrix multiplications over batches of images. After this, computer vision, and soon the rest of AI, moved to deep networks on GPUs. In 2025 the Computer History Museum, together with Google, published the original source code.
history.cudnn.title: cuDNN: the primitives in one library
history.cudnn.alt: A convolution lowered to a matrix multiplication (GEMM)
history.cudnn.p1: By 2014 every lab was writing its own GPU convolution kernels. NVIDIA's cuDNN (Chetlur et al., 2014) packaged the primitives of deep learning, convolution, pooling, normalisation and activations, as tuned library calls on 4-D tensors in layouts such as NCHW (batch, channels, height, width).
history.cudnn.p2: Its main strategy lowers a convolution to a matrix multiplication (GEMM) without ever building the full unrolled matrix in memory; later versions added FFT and Winograd algorithms. Caffe, Theano and Torch adopted it quickly, and from then on the speed of a deep-learning framework largely meant the speed of a handful of tensor kernels: the same lesson as BLAS in the Coding Skills page.
history.tensorflow.title: TensorFlow: the name says it
history.tensorflow.alt: Tensors flowing through a dataflow graph
history.tensorflow.p1: On 9 November 2015 Google open-sourced TensorFlow, the successor of its internal DistBelief system. A program was a dataflow graph: nodes are operations and edges carry tensors, multidimensional arrays, and the graph could be placed on CPUs, GPUs and later TPUs, across many machines. Tensors, flowing through a graph.
history.tensorflow.p2: The tensor of deep learning is mostly the array of numbers rather than the geometric object with its transformation rules; but the habit of naming axes and contracting them is Ricci's. TensorFlow 2 (2019) made eager execution the default, partly in answer to PyTorch.
history.tpu.title: TPU: a systolic array for matrices
history.tpu.p1: In May 2016 Google revealed that since 2015 it had been running its own chip in its data centres: the Tensor Processing Unit. The 2017 ISCA paper by Norman Jouppi and colleagues described its heart, the Matrix Multiply Unit: a 256 × 256 systolic array of 65,536 8-bit multiply–accumulate cells. Weights stay in the cells while activations flow through them in waves, so every value fetched from memory is reused many times.
history.tpu.p2: The first TPU did inference only, with a peak of 92 trillion operations per second; on Google's own workloads it was on average about 15 to 30 times faster than the contemporary CPU and GPU, and 30 to 80 times better in performance per watt. Later generations added training and the bfloat16 floating-point format. The picture shows a TPU v3 board.
history.nvlink.title: NVLink and NVSwitch: many GPUs as one
history.nvlink.alt: The Tesla P100 (GP100) chip with its HBM2 memory stacks
history.nvlink.p1: Large models outgrew one GPU, and the PCIe bus became the bottleneck. NVIDIA announced NVLink in 2014; it first shipped in 2016 in the Tesla P100 (Pascal), whose four links gave up to 160 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth to other GPUs, about five times a PCIe 3.0 ×16 slot. The P100 also put stacked HBM2 memory right next to the chip, as in the picture.
history.nvlink.p2: In 2018 NVSwitch turned point-to-point links into a switch fabric: in the DGX-2, twelve switch chips let 16 V100 GPUs talk to each other at full NVLink speed. Later generations scaled the idea to whole racks, with 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain in 2024's GB200 NVL72. For tensor programs this is what makes it practical to split one huge matrix multiplication across many GPUs and add up the pieces with an all-reduce.
history.dgx1.title: DGX-1 goes to OpenAI
history.dgx1.p1: In April 2016 NVIDIA announced the DGX-1: eight P100 GPUs joined by NVLink in one box, with a list price of 129,000 US dollars. On 15 August 2016 Jensen Huang personally delivered the first unit to OpenAI, then a young non-profit lab in San Francisco, signed with "I present you the world's first DGX-1!".
history.dgx1.p2: OpenAI's Ilya Sutskever said it would shorten experiments by weeks. OpenAI later scaled to thousands of GPUs, and the language models that followed are, at heart, enormous chains of the same tensor contractions as in Part I, running on hardware descended from that box.
history.pytorch.title: PyTorch: tensors you can print
history.pytorch.alt: Operations recorded on a tape, then differentiated backwards
history.pytorch.p1: At Facebook AI Research, Adam Paszke (then an intern), Sam Gross, Soumith Chintala and Gregory Chanan rebuilt the Lua-based Torch for Python; the first public release came in January 2017. Instead of building a graph first and running it later, PyTorch runs each operation at once (define-by-run, an idea it shared with Chainer) and records it on a tape for automatic differentiation. You could debug a network with `print()`.
history.pytorch.p2: Researchers moved over in large numbers; the 2019 NeurIPS paper describes the design. In 2022 PyTorch moved to the vendor-neutral PyTorch Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Its core object, `torch.Tensor`, is what every problem on this site computes with.
history.v100.title: Volta V100: Tensor Cores
history.v100.alt: A Tensor Core computes $D = AB + C$ on $4 \times 4$ tiles
history.v100.p1: In May 2017 NVIDIA announced the Volta V100: 21.1 billion transistors on an 815 mm² die and, for the first time, 640 Tensor Cores. Each Tensor Core performs a small matrix multiply–accumulate, $D = AB + C$ on $4 \times 4$ matrices, every clock cycle, with FP16 inputs and products accumulated in FP16 or FP32. Together they deliver up to 125 teraFLOPS for deep learning.
history.v100.p2: Tensor Cores are dedicated matrix multiply–accumulate units inside each streaming multiprocessor, fed by warps of threads; unlike the TPU's Matrix Multiply Unit they are not a large systolic array. Libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN use them when shapes and data types allow, which is why mixed precision (16-bit inputs, 32-bit accumulation) became the standard way to train.
history.m1.title: Apple M1: one memory for everything
history.m1.alt: Illustration of the Apple M1 package with its two memory chips
history.m1.p1: In November 2020 Apple introduced the M1, its first chip for the Mac: 16 billion transistors on a 5 nm process, with CPU, GPU and a 16-core Neural Engine (up to 11 trillion operations per second) on one die, and the memory in the same package. In this unified memory architecture all of them work on the same buffers, so a tensor does not have to be copied between CPU memory and GPU memory.
history.m1.p2: The CPU cluster also contains an undocumented matrix coprocessor, known as AMX (present since the A13 phone chip), which independent researchers have reverse-engineered and which Apple exposes through its Accelerate framework. Since PyTorch 1.12 (2022) the `mps` device runs tensors on the M-series GPU, one reason this site runs natively on Macs.
history.einsum.title: Finale: one line, a century-long relay
history.einsum.alt: The contraction $C_{ik} = A_{ij} B_{jk}$ written as `einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)`
history.einsum.p1: Today, when you write `torch.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)`, you call on a relay that has run for almost two centuries: Gauss's insight that geometry can be measured from inside, Riemann's metric, Christoffel's symbols, Ricci's indices, Einstein dropping the $\sum$, and then GPUs, datasets, Tensor Cores, systolic arrays and NVLink that carry out the same contraction $C_{ik} = A_{ij} B_{jk}$ billions of times a second.
history.einsum.p2: On the Coding Skills page, the index contractions this story has followed (dot products, matrix products, sums over a shared index, even the Lorentz transformation of Minkowski's field tensor, `torch.einsum("ma,nb,ab->mn", L, L, F)`) are each written as one line of einsum. A notation invented for curved spacetime turned out to be the language of machines that learn.
history.fun.title: 💡 Did you know?
history.fun.heliotrope: While leading the land survey of Hanover, Gauss invented the heliotrope (1821): a mirror instrument that flashes sunlight to a station tens of kilometres away, so that it can be sighted precisely. On cloudy days the survey simply had to wait.
history.fun.habilitation: Riemann proposed three topics for his Habilitation lecture and, as was usual, expected one of the first two to be chosen; against his expectation Gauss chose the third, geometry. According to Wilhelm Weber, as reported by Dedekind, Gauss praised the lecture on the way home with an emotion he rarely showed.
history.fun.hilbert: David Hilbert submitted his own paper on 20 November 1915, five days before Einstein's final paper of 25 November. In 1997 historians found that Hilbert's surviving printer's proofs, dated 6 December, do not show the final field equations explicitly; but part of one page has been cut off, so who was first is still argued over.
history.fun.brook: Before CUDA, researchers did matrix maths on GPUs by disguising it as graphics: the numbers were stored as the pixels of a texture and computed by shader programs. Ian Buck's Brook project at Stanford (BrookGPU) made this much easier to program, and Buck then took the idea to NVIDIA.
history.fun.mythbusters: At NVIDIA's NVISION conference in 2008, MythBusters' Adam Savage and Jamie Hyneman explained CPU versus GPU with paintball robots. A small robot painted a smiley face one shot at a time; then a huge rig with more than a thousand barrels painted the Mona Lisa in a fraction of a second.
history.fun.dennys: NVIDIA was planned in a booth at a Denny's diner in San Jose. Since 2023 a plaque there marks "the booth that launched a \$1 trillion company"; Jensen Huang had once worked at Denny's himself, as a dishwasher and busboy.
history.fun.alexnet: AlexNet was trained on two gaming GPUs (GeForce GTX 580, 3 GB each) for five to six days, at Krizhevsky's parents' house. The network was split across the two cards because it did not fit in the memory of one; in 2025 the Computer History Museum released the original source code.
history.fun.dgx1: Jensen Huang delivered the first DGX-1 to OpenAI in person and signed it: "To the future of computing and humanity. I present you the world's first DGX-1!"
history.fun.alphago: Google's TPU was already running AlphaGo when it beat Lee Sedol in March 2016. Google revealed the chip only two months later, in May 2016.

nvlink.title: NVLink & NVSwitch: principles and programming
nvlink.intro: A model too large for one GPU has to split its tensors over several GPUs, and then every training step also moves tensors between them. NVLink is NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link; NVSwitch is the switch chip that joins many GPUs over NVLink. This tab explains why they exist, how fast each generation is, how GPUs are wired together, which collective operations run over the links, and how PyTorch uses them through NCCL.
nvlink.howto: Bandwidths are in GB/s ($1\ \text{GB} = 10^9$ bytes). NVIDIA quotes NVLink bandwidth per GPU with **both directions added** (bidirectional); one transfer from GPU A to GPU B gets at most half of it. Every table column says which of the two it shows, and every number links to the NVIDIA, NCCL or PyTorch document it comes from.
nvlink.why.title: Why GPUs need a fast interconnect
nvlink.why.text: Inside one GPU, tensors stream from HBM memory at terabytes per second. Between GPUs, the classic path is the PCIe bus, which is more than 20 times slower than the GPU's own memory. When a training step has to exchange gigabytes between GPUs, that link, not the arithmetic, sets the pace. NVLink closes most of the gap: on an H100, NVLink 4 moves 900 GB/s per GPU, which NVIDIA quotes as over 7 times PCIe Gen5.
nvlink.why.bar.caption: One H100 SXM GPU: PCIe Gen5 x16 (128 GB/s) and NVLink 4 (900 GB/s) with both directions added, and the GPU's own HBM3 memory bandwidth (3,350 GB/s). Fixed axis from 0 to 3,500 GB/s.
nvlink.why.timeTitle: Where multi-GPU training spends its communication time
nvlink.why.dp: **Data parallel.** Every GPU holds the whole model and a slice of the batch. After `backward()` the gradients of all GPUs are summed with an **all-reduce**: every step moves about twice the gradient size per GPU (2 bytes per parameter in bf16, so about 2 GB of gradients for a 1-billion-parameter model).
nvlink.why.tp: **Tensor parallel.** One layer's weight matrices are split over GPUs (columns on one, rows on another), so each layer ends with an all-reduce or all-gather of **activations**, in the forward and in the backward pass. This traffic sits on the critical path of every layer, which is why tensor parallelism is kept inside an NVLink domain.
nvlink.why.pp: **Pipeline parallel.** Consecutive layers live on different GPUs and only the activations at a stage boundary are sent, point to point, to the next GPU. Less data than tensor parallel, but GPUs wait for each other (the pipeline "bubble"), so a fast link still shortens each hand-over.
nvlink.gens.title: NVLink generations
nvlink.gens.text: Each generation either added links per GPU or made each link faster. From NVLink 2 to NVLink 4 one link carried 25 GB/s in each direction and the GPU got more links (6, 12, 18); NVLink 5 doubled the per-link rate. PCIe x16 doubled per generation too, but from a much lower start.
nvlink.gens.table.title: NVLink 1 to 5 and PCIe Gen3 to Gen6 x16: links and bandwidth per GPU
nvlink.gens.table.note: NVLink 1 and NVLink 5: NVIDIA states 40 GB/s and 100 GB/s per link with both directions added; the one-direction column is half of that. PCIe Gen3 and Gen4 x16 carry 15.75 and 31.5 GB/s in each direction (often rounded to 16 and 32); Gen5 carries 64 GB/s each way (128 GB/s total) and Gen6 256 GB/s total. P100 memory: 732 GB/s in the Volta whitepaper (the P100 overview rounds to 720).

nvlink.topo.title: Topologies: mesh, switch and rack
nvlink.topo.text: A GPU has a fixed number of NVLinks, so how the links are wired decides who can talk to whom at full speed. With **point-to-point links** (a mesh) each GPU reaches only its direct neighbours; any other pair either takes two hops or falls back to PCIe. With an **NVSwitch** every GPU connects its links to switch chips, and every pair of GPUs talks at the GPU's full NVLink bandwidth, all at the same time (all-to-all).
nvlink.topo.svg.switchHops: GPU 0 → GPU 5: 1 hop via the switch
nvlink.topo.svg.caption: Left: 8 GPUs with 4 NVLinks each (16 links): two fully connected groups of 4 (front and back face of the cube, with diagonals) plus one link from each GPU to its partner in the other group. GPU 0 and GPU 5 share no link, so their data goes via GPU 4 (amber). Right: every GPU's links go to the NVSwitch (drawn as one box; real systems use several switch chips), so every pair is one hop apart at full bandwidth.
nvlink.topo.dgx1.tip: 2016 · 8 × Tesla P100 · 4 NVLinks per GPU · hybrid cube-mesh
nvlink.topo.dgx1.text: The first DGX-1 (2016) joined eight Tesla P100 GPUs with NVLink in a **hybrid cube-mesh**, the left diagram. The V100 version kept the same topology with 6 links per GPU. Fast inside each group of four, but collectives must be routed around the cube.
nvlink.topo.dgx2.tip: 2018 · 16 × V100 32 GB · 12 NVSwitches (6 per board) · 18 NVLink ports per switch at 51.5 GB/s · 2.4 TB/s bisection bandwidth
nvlink.topo.dgx2.text: **NVSwitch** (2018) is a switch chip with 18 NVLink ports. The DGX-2 used twelve of them, six on each of two boards, to join 16 V100 GPUs so that any GPU reaches any other at full NVLink bandwidth: 2.4 TB/s of bisection bandwidth. The later 8-GPU HGX boards (A100, H100, B200) also use NVSwitch, as in the right diagram.
nvlink.topo.nvl72.tip: Hopper: NVLink Switch System up to 256 GPUs · GB200 NVL72: 72 Blackwell GPUs in one NVLink domain, 1.8 TB/s per GPU, 130 TB/s in total
nvlink.topo.nvl72.text: The **NVLink Switch System** takes NVSwitch out of the box: switch trays connect GPUs in different servers over NVLink. NVIDIA describes up to 256 GPUs for Hopper; the **GB200 NVL72** rack puts 72 Blackwell GPUs into one NVLink domain with 130 TB/s of total NVLink bandwidth, so tensor parallelism can span a whole rack.
nvlink.topo.geforce.tip: RTX 2080 / 2080 Ti: NVLink bridge · RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti: NVLink (SLI-ready): Yes · RTX 4090: NVLink (SLI-ready): No
nvlink.topo.geforce.text: **Consumer cards** are different: no NVSwitch, at most a two-card NVLink bridge. NVIDIA lists the bridge for the GeForce RTX 2080 and 2080 Ti and NVLink for the RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti; the RTX 4090 specification says NVLink: No. Multi-GPU work on such cards goes over PCIe.
nvlink.coll.title: Collectives: what happens to the tensors
nvlink.coll.text: Multi-GPU programs rarely send single messages; they call **collectives**, operations in which all $N$ GPUs take part and each ends with a defined piece of the result. Below, $S$ is the size of the full tensor; the last column is how many bytes each GPU must send, as a multiple of $S$, with the bandwidth-optimal ring algorithm (NCCL's "bus bandwidth" factor).
nvlink.coll.allreduce.name: All-reduce
nvlink.coll.allreduce.what: Element-wise sum (or max, ...) of the tensors of all GPUs; every GPU gets the whole result. Used for gradient averaging in data parallel training.
nvlink.coll.allgather.name: All-gather
nvlink.coll.allgather.what: Every GPU contributes one slice; every GPU gets all slices concatenated. Used to rebuild sharded weights (FSDP, ZeRO).
nvlink.coll.reducescatter.name: Reduce-scatter
nvlink.coll.reducescatter.what: Sum over the GPUs like all-reduce, but GPU $i$ keeps only slice $i$ of the result. Used for sharded gradients (FSDP, ZeRO).
nvlink.coll.broadcast.name: Broadcast
nvlink.coll.broadcast.what: One GPU (the root) sends its tensor to all others. Used for the initial weights, so every replica starts the same.
nvlink.anim.start: Start: GPU i holds its own vector, split into 4 chunks
nvlink.anim.rs: Reduce-scatter, step {k} of {n}: send one chunk to the right neighbour, add it
nvlink.anim.ag: All-gather, step {k} of {n}: pass the finished chunks on, copy them
nvlink.anim.done: Done: every GPU holds the full sum Σ = a+b+c+d of every chunk
nvlink.anim.caption: Ring all-reduce on 4 GPUs holding the vectors a, b, c, d, each cut into 4 chunks (rows 0 to 3). In every step each GPU sends one chunk to its right neighbour (amber arrows; the last GPU wraps round to GPU 0). After $N-1 = 3$ reduce-scatter steps each GPU owns one fully summed chunk; $3$ all-gather steps then copy those chunks round the ring. Each GPU sent $2(N-1) = 6$ chunks of size $S/N$, that is $\tfrac{2(N-1)}{N}S$, and all links were busy in every step.
nvlink.coll.eqText: $S$: bytes to reduce, $N$: GPUs, $B$: link bandwidth in one direction (bytes/s), $\alpha$: fixed latency per step. For large tensors the bandwidth term dominates, and it hardly grows with $N$: the factor $\tfrac{2(N-1)}{N}$ goes from 1 (2 GPUs) to almost 2. That is why the ring is called bandwidth-optimal. Its weakness is the latency term, which grows linearly with $N$.
nvlink.coll.tree: A tree reduces up to a root and broadcasts back down, so it needs only about $2\log_2 N$ steps instead of $2(N-1)$. NCCL 2.4 added **double binary trees**, which keep the full bandwidth while their latency grows logarithmically; NVIDIA measured up to 180 times faster all-reduce than rings at 24,000 GPUs on the Summit supercomputer. For large messages on a few GPUs the ring is as good, and NCCL switches back to rings where they give more bandwidth.
nvlink.coll.ncclTitle: How NCCL picks NVLink, PCIe or the network
nvlink.coll.nccl: NCCL (the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, PyTorch's GPU backend) detects the topology when the process group starts: which GPUs share NVLink or NVSwitch, which only share a PCIe switch or CPU socket, and which network cards (InfiniBand, RoCE, Ethernet) sit near which GPU. It then builds rings and trees over the fastest paths (inside a server over NVLink or PCIe peer-to-peer, between servers over the network) and chooses the algorithm per message size (`NCCL_ALGO`: Ring, Tree, and newer ones such as NVLS on NVSwitch systems). You normally leave all of this automatic; environment variables such as `NCCL_ALGO` and `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE` exist for experiments and debugging.
nvlink.code.title: Programming: PyTorch, NCCL and the tools
nvlink.code.text: In PyTorch you rarely touch NVLink directly: `torch.distributed` with the `nccl` backend runs the collectives, NCCL routes them over NVLink when it is there, and `torchrun` starts one process per GPU. The same script works on a PCIe-only machine, only slower.
nvlink.code.shown: These examples are **shown, not run**: the machine that builds this site has a single GPU, so there is no NVLink to measure. Only the last, single-process example runs anywhere.
nvlink.code.smi: Checking the topology and NCCL's choices (shell)
nvlink.code.gloo: Try the API on one machine: world size 1, gloo backend
nvlink.code.glooText: With one process every collective returns its input, but the calls are the same as on 8 GPUs, so you can write and test the code path on a laptop before running it with `torchrun` and `nccl`.
nvlink.code.moreTitle: Further reading: CUDA-aware MPI and NVSHMEM
nvlink.code.more: Outside PyTorch, **CUDA-aware MPI** lets an MPI program pass GPU buffers straight to `MPI_Send` or `MPI_Allreduce` without copying them to host memory first, and the library uses NVLink or GPUDirect underneath. **NVSHMEM** goes further: GPU threads read and write other GPUs' memory from inside a kernel (a partitioned global address space), which suits fine-grained communication that would be too small for collectives.
nvlink.practice.title: When NVLink matters, and a worked example
nvlink.practice.matters: Large models that need **tensor parallelism** (activations exchanged in every layer), sharded training (FSDP, ZeRO) with frequent all-gathers and reduce-scatters, mixture-of-experts models whose all-to-all token routing is bandwidth bound, and data parallel training whose gradient all-reduce takes as long as the compute of one step.
nvlink.practice.fine: Data parallel training of **small models** (megabytes to a few hundred megabytes of gradients, and DDP overlaps their all-reduce with the backward pass), **inference** where each GPU serves its own copy of the model, and independent jobs, one per GPU (hyperparameter sweeps). Here the GPUs barely talk, and NVLink would sit idle.
nvlink.practice.worked: **Worked example.** All-reduce of 1 GB of gradients over 8 GPUs: each GPU sends $\tfrac{2 \cdot 7}{8} \cdot 1\ \text{GB} = 1.75\ \text{GB}$. Over PCIe Gen4 x16 at 32 GB/s per direction the cost model predicts **{pcie}**; over NVLink 4 (H100, 450 GB/s per direction) **{nvl}**, about {ratio} times faster. If one training step computes for 50 ms, the first case more than doubles the step time while the second adds less than a tenth.
nvlink.calc.title: Cost model calculator (bandwidth term only)
nvlink.calc.note: $t = \tfrac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot S / B$ with the per-GPU NVLink bandwidth in one direction (half of the table's both-direction total), as on an NVSwitch system. Ideal values: no latency term, no protocol overhead, no contention. With PCIe the GPUs often share switches or cross the CPU, so measured times are longer.
nvlink.practice.caveat: To check a real machine, run the `all_reduce_perf` benchmark from NVIDIA's nccl-tests: it prints the "bus bandwidth", the measured counterpart of $B$ above, which you can plug into the formula. Compare it with the table: a big gap usually means the traffic is not on the path you expect, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` shows which one NCCL took.
nvlink.anim.codeNotes: What the code does, line by line
nvlink.anim.path.title: Two ways from GPU 0 to GPU 1
nvlink.anim.path.s0: **PCIe.** Without NVLink, data leaves GPU 0 through its PCIe slot, passes a PCIe switch (or the CPU) and enters GPU 1: at most 64 GB/s each way for PCIe Gen5 x16.
nvlink.anim.path.s1: **NVLink.** A direct GPU-to-GPU link: on an H100, 450 GB/s each way (900 GB/s with both directions added), about 7 times more. More squares in flight means more bytes per second; each square travels at the same speed.
nvlink.anim.path.s2: **Race for 1 GB.** Ideal time to move $10^9$ bytes one way: $1/64$ s $\approx$ 15.6 ms over PCIe Gen5, $1/450$ s $\approx$ 2.2 ms over NVLink 4.
nvlink.anim.path.caption: Bandwidths of one H100 SXM from the table below (NVIDIA Hopper documents), one direction. Times are ideal (bandwidth only, no latency or protocol overhead). Fixed time axis from 0 to 16 ms.
nvlink.anim.path.axis: time to move 1 GB one way (ms, ideal)
nvlink.anim.parallel.title: Three ways to split a model over GPUs
nvlink.anim.parallel.s0: **Data parallel.** Both GPUs hold the whole weight matrix $W$ and get half of the batch $X$ each. Each computes its own gradient $\partial W$ (different colours); an all-reduce sums them, so both apply the same update. Traffic: the gradients, once per step.
nvlink.anim.parallel.s1: **Tensor parallel.** $W$ is split by columns: GPU 0 holds the left half, GPU 1 the right half. Both get the same $X$, each computes half of the output $Y = XW$, and an all-gather joins the halves. Traffic: activations, in every layer.
nvlink.anim.parallel.s2: **Pipeline parallel.** Layer 1 lives on GPU 0, layer 2 on GPU 1. GPU 0 computes the activations $H$ and sends them to GPU 1, which computes the next layer. Traffic: only the activations at the boundary, point to point.
nvlink.anim.parallel.caption: Two GPUs and 4 × 4 matrices; dashed cells are parts a GPU does not hold. Arrows: data crossing the GPU-to-GPU link, which NVLink makes fast.
nvlink.anim.gens.title: Bandwidth per GPU = links × rate per link
nvlink.anim.gens.s0: **NVLink 1** (Tesla P100, 2016): 4 links × 40 GB/s = 160 GB/s per GPU, both directions added.
nvlink.anim.gens.s2: **NVLink 3** (A100, 2020): the same rate per link, twice the links: 12 × 50 = 600 GB/s.
nvlink.anim.gens.s4: **NVLink 5** (B200, 2024): still 18 links, each twice as fast: 18 × 100 = 1,800 GB/s.
nvlink.anim.gens.s5: **PCIe x16** for comparison (grey): 32, 64, 128 and 256 GB/s for Gen3 to Gen6, both directions added.
nvlink.anim.gens.caption: Each segment of a bar is one link, both directions added (twice the one-direction rate in the table below). Fixed axis from 0 to 2,000 GB/s. Numbers from the NVIDIA documents cited in the table.
nvlink.anim.hops.title: Hops between GPUs: mesh vs switch
nvlink.anim.hops.s0: **Neighbours** (GPU 0 → GPU 1): a direct link in the mesh, one hop through the switch. Same speed.
nvlink.anim.hops.s1: **Not neighbours** (GPU 0 → GPU 5): the mesh has no link, so the data goes via GPU 4 (red). Two links are busy and GPU 4 has to forward the data. Through the NVSwitch it is still one hop.
nvlink.anim.hops.s2: **All 28 pairs**, one after another: in the cube-mesh 16 pairs are neighbours and 12 need two hops; with the NVSwitch every pair is one hop, at full bandwidth.
nvlink.anim.hops.caption: Left: the DGX-1 hybrid cube-mesh (8 GPUs, 4 NVLinks each). Right: an 8-GPU NVSwitch system (drawn as one switch; real boards use several switch chips). Hop counts computed by breadth-first search over the links.
nvlink.anim.colls.title: The four collectives, before and after
nvlink.anim.colls.s0: **All-reduce**: every GPU starts with its own vector (a, b, c, d) and ends with the element-wise sum Σ of all four.
nvlink.anim.colls.s1: **All-gather**: GPU $i$ starts with one slice; afterwards every GPU holds all four slices.
nvlink.anim.colls.s2: **Reduce-scatter**: like all-reduce, but GPU $i$ keeps only slice $i$ of the sum.
nvlink.anim.colls.s3: **Broadcast**: GPU 0's vector is copied to every GPU.
nvlink.anim.colls.caption: 4 GPUs, each tensor in 4 slices (columns). Letters: whose data a slice holds (a from GPU 0, b from GPU 1, and so on); Σ: the sum over all GPUs. An all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, which is exactly how the ring below does it.
nvlink.anim.tree.title: Ring or tree: number of steps for 8 GPUs
nvlink.anim.tree.s0: **Ring**: $N - 1 = 7$ reduce-scatter steps (amber) and 7 all-gather steps (green), 14 in all. In every step all links are busy, which gives the full bandwidth, but every step also costs a fixed latency.
nvlink.anim.tree.s1: **Tree**: partial sums flow up to the root in $\log_2 8 = 3$ steps (amber) and the result flows back down in 3 more (green): 6 steps. With many GPUs the gap grows: $2(N-1)$ against about $2\log_2 N$.
nvlink.anim.tree.caption: One binary tree, to count the steps. NCCL uses two binary trees at once (a double binary tree) so that every GPU sends and receives at full bandwidth, and picks ring or tree per message size.
nvlink.anim.ddp.title: What DDP does in one training step
nvlink.anim.ddp.s0: **Own mini-batch.** `torchrun` starts one process per GPU; each holds a full copy of the model (layers L1 to L3) and gets different input data.
nvlink.anim.ddp.s1: **Forward.** Each GPU runs its batch through the layers and computes its own `loss`. No communication yet.
nvlink.anim.ddp.s2: **Backward with overlap.** `loss.backward()` computes gradients from the last layer to the first. DDP groups them in buckets and starts an all-reduce for each bucket as soon as it is ready (arrows), while the earlier layers are still computing.
nvlink.anim.ddp.s3: **Step.** After the all-reduce both GPUs hold the same averaged gradients, so `opt.step()` makes the same update and the copies stay identical.
nvlink.anim.ddp.caption: Two GPUs and three layers, one bucket per layer for simplicity (DDP's default bucket size is 25 MB). The all-reduce runs over NCCL, on NVLink when there is one.
nvlink.anim.p2p.title: Three routes for `x.to("cuda:1")`
nvlink.anim.p2p.s0: **NVLink peer-to-peer.** If the two GPUs share NVLink, the copy goes straight across it.
nvlink.anim.p2p.s1: **PCIe peer-to-peer.** Without NVLink but with peer access (`can_device_access_peer` returns `True`), the copy crosses the PCIe switch directly from GPU to GPU.
nvlink.anim.p2p.s2: **Staged through host memory.** Without peer access the copy goes GPU 0 → host memory, then host memory → GPU 1: two transfers, both over PCIe, with the CPU's memory in between.
nvlink.anim.p2p.caption: Ideal times for 1 GiB ($2^{30}$ bytes) with the H100 numbers of the table: NVLink 4 at 450 GB/s and PCIe Gen5 at 64 GB/s, one direction.
nvlink.anim.overlap.title: The worked example as a time line
nvlink.anim.overlap.s0: **PCIe Gen4, one after the other.** 50 ms of compute, then the all-reduce of 1 GB over 8 GPUs: 54.7 ms. The step more than doubles.
nvlink.anim.overlap.s1: **NVLink 4.** The same all-reduce takes 3.9 ms; the step grows by less than a tenth.
nvlink.anim.overlap.s2: **Overlap.** DDP starts the all-reduce while backward is still running. If backward is two thirds of the compute, NVLink's communication is hidden completely; PCIe's is still longer than backward and sticks out.
nvlink.anim.overlap.caption: Cost model of this card (bandwidth term only, 1 GB, 8 GPUs, ring all-reduce). The two-thirds backward share in step 3 is an illustrative assumption. Fixed time axis from 0 to 120 ms.
nvlink.anim.code.ddp.0: `torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py` starts 8 copies of the script, one per GPU, and tells each its rank (its number) through environment variables.
nvlink.anim.code.ddp.1: `dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")` connects the 8 processes; NCCL carries the GPU-to-GPU traffic, over NVLink if there is one.
nvlink.anim.code.ddp.2: `LOCAL_RANK` and `torch.cuda.set_device(rank)` give each process its own GPU, so process 3 works on GPU 3.
nvlink.anim.code.ddp.3: `dist.all_reduce(g, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)`: each process starts with a tensor full of its rank (0 to 7); afterwards every process holds the sum $0 + 1 + \dots + 7 = 28$.
nvlink.anim.code.ddp.4: `DDP(...)` wraps the model so that `loss.backward()` also all-reduces the gradients across the processes (the animation below).
nvlink.anim.code.ddp.5: `opt.step()` then applies identical gradients on every GPU, and `dist.destroy_process_group()` closes the connections.
nvlink.anim.code.p2p.0: `torch.cuda.device_count()` prints how many GPUs PyTorch can see.
nvlink.anim.code.p2p.1: `torch.cuda.can_device_access_peer(0, 1)` is `True` if GPU 0 can read and write GPU 1's memory directly (over NVLink or PCIe), without going through the CPU.
nvlink.anim.code.p2p.2: `torch.randn(256, 1024, 1024, device="cuda:0")` creates $256 \times 1024 \times 1024$ float32 numbers of 4 bytes each: 1 GiB on GPU 0.
nvlink.anim.code.p2p.3: `x.to("cuda:1")` copies it to GPU 1 by the fastest route available (animation below); `torch.cuda.synchronize()` waits until the copy has finished, which matters when you time it.
nvlink.anim.code.smi.0: `nvidia-smi topo -m` prints a matrix of how each pair of GPUs (and network cards) is connected: `NV#` means # NVLinks; `PIX` at most one PCIe bridge, `PXB` several PCIe bridges, `PHB` through a PCIe host bridge (the CPU), `NODE` between host bridges of one CPU, `SYS` across the link between CPU sockets.
nvlink.anim.code.smi.1: `nvidia-smi nvlink --status` lists each GPU's NVLinks and their speed; links that are down or missing show up here.
nvlink.anim.code.smi.2: `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` makes NCCL log what it detected and chose: the topology, the rings and trees, and the transport (`P2P` over NVLink or PCIe, `SHM` through host memory, `NET` over the network).
nvlink.anim.code.smi.3: `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1` forbids direct GPU-to-GPU transfers; running the job once with it and once without shows how much the direct path is worth.
nvlink.anim.code.gloo.0: `dist.init_process_group("gloo", ...)` starts a process group with the CPU backend gloo, a single process (`world_size=1`, `rank=0`) and a local address to meet at; no GPU needed.
nvlink.anim.code.gloo.2: `dist.all_reduce(t)` sums `t` over all processes; with one process the sum is `t` itself, so it is unchanged.
nvlink.anim.code.gloo.3: `dist.get_world_size()` returns 1, and `dist.destroy_process_group()` cleans up. Swap in `"nccl"` and `torchrun` to run the same calls on many GPUs.
cpuml.title: Migrating CPU-only ML to tensors
cpuml.intro: Many classical machine-learning tools, scikit-learn first among them, run only on the CPU. Their maths is mostly linear algebra over all data points at once, which is exactly what tensor code does well. This tab migrates six of them (PCA, linear and kernel SVMs, logistic regression, k nearest neighbours and k-means) to PyTorch tensor code that runs on the CPU or the GPU, and checks every one against scikit-learn on the same data.
cpuml.howto: Each card: the maths in vector and index form, the scikit-learn call next to the tensor code (both exactly as timed), what changes in the move, the agreement on MNIST digits (accuracy, objective value, explained variance) and the measured speed-up over scikit-learn on synthetic data of growing size. Then UMAP as a full case study, and RAPIDS cuML, the ready-made GPU version of scikit-learn.
cpuml.why.title: Why and how to migrate
cpuml.why.sklearn: **What scikit-learn is.** The reference library for classical machine learning in Python: one consistent `fit` / `predict` interface, careful defaults, and solvers in compiled C, C++ and Cython (LAPACK, liblinear, libsvm, OpenMP). It runs on the CPU only, on one machine, and for small and medium data it is hard to beat there.
cpuml.why.gain: **Why move to tensors.** The same model as tensor code runs on the GPU unchanged, handles many problems at once (a batch dimension), gets its gradients from autograd, and plugs into a larger PyTorch pipeline (feature extractor, loss, training loop) without copying arrays back to NumPy.
cpuml.why.recipe: **The recipe.** 1. Write the objective or update rule in index form. 2. Turn every sum into a matrix product, `einsum` or reduction, and every loop over points into broadcasting. 3. Replace the special-purpose solver by a generic one on the same objective (L-BFGS, projected gradient). 4. Test against scikit-learn on the same data: accuracy, objective value, predictions.
cpuml.why.honest: **What to expect.** Same objective, not the same algorithm: SMO, liblinear and tree searches are clever sequential methods, and the tensor versions trade them for many dense steps that suit a GPU. On small data scikit-learn often wins (no launch overhead, highly tuned C). Tensors win when N is large, when there is a GPU, or when many models train together. The measurements below show both.
cpuml.changes: What changes when you move to tensors
cpuml.agree.title: Agreement on MNIST ({train} digits to train, {test} to test; same data, same objective)
cpuml.metric.evr_sum: explained variance ratio, sum over the kept components
cpuml.metric.evr_maxdiff: largest difference in explained variance ratio from scikit-learn
cpuml.metric.coef_rel_diff: largest coefficient difference, relative to the largest coefficient
cpuml.chart.title: Speed-up over scikit-learn (log scale)
cpuml.chart.range: Bar: scikit-learn time / tensor time, median of the passes, from 1× (equal); error bar |–|: from the least to the most favourable pass. Synthetic data; times include the whole fit.
cpuml.pca.title: PCA: centring by broadcasting, one SVD
cpuml.pca.text: Principal component analysis finds the orthogonal directions of largest variance. scikit-learn's `PCA(svd_solver="full")` centres the data and calls LAPACK's singular value decomposition; the tensor version is the same two steps written out: subtract the column means (one broadcast) and call `torch.linalg.svd`. On MNIST it keeps $k = {k}$ components of the 784 pixel features.
cpuml.pca.changes: Centring becomes broadcasting: `X - X.mean(dim=0)` subtracts a (D,) row from every row of an (N, D) matrix, with no loop. The decomposition is one library call, so on the CPU both versions end in the same kind of LAPACK routine; what the tensor version adds is the device (the same line runs on the GPU through cuSOLVER), batching (`torch.linalg.svd` accepts a stack (B, N, D) of data sets) and a place inside a larger tensor pipeline. Singular vectors are defined only up to sign, so compare $|\cos|$ between components, never the raw components. For a few components of a very large matrix, `torch.pca_lowrank` (randomised SVD) is the counterpart of `svd_solver="randomized"`.
cpuml.linsvm.title: Linear SVM: liblinear's objective, minimised by L-BFGS
cpuml.linsvm.text: A linear support vector machine separates classes by hyperplanes with a margin. scikit-learn's `LinearSVC` calls liblinear (coordinate descent on the dual), one binary problem per digit (one-vs-rest). Its default loss is the squared hinge, and liblinear penalises the bias like a weight. The tensor version minimises exactly that objective, with $C = {C}$, by full-batch L-BFGS on tensors.
cpuml.linsvm.changes: The solver changes, the objective does not. Instead of liblinear's coordinate updates, write the loss as one tensor expression and hand it to a generic optimiser (`torch.optim.LBFGS` with autograd). The ten one-vs-rest problems become one (D+1, 10) weight matrix trained at once: their objectives are independent, so the sum has the same minimiser as each alone. A column of ones reproduces liblinear's penalised bias. The squared hinge is differentiable, so L-BFGS converges cleanly; the plain hinge (`loss="hinge"`) is not, and would need a subgradient method or the dual.
cpuml.ksvm.title: Kernel SVM: a broadcast kernel matrix and the dual problem
cpuml.ksvm.text: A kernel SVM draws curved boundaries by comparing points through a kernel: here the Gaussian (RBF) kernel with scikit-learn's `gamma="scale"` and $C = {C}$, on a binary task (even against odd digits). scikit-learn's `SVC` runs libsvm's SMO, which updates two multipliers at a time and computes kernel rows on demand. We do not reimplement SMO. The tensor version builds the whole kernel matrix by broadcasting and maximises the same dual problem by accelerated projected gradient ascent.
cpuml.ksvm.changes: The kernel matrix $K_{ij} = e^{-\gamma \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2}$ is one broadcast expression: $\lVert x_i \rVert^2 + \lVert x_j \rVert^2 - 2\, x_i \cdot x_j$ through a matrix product, then `exp`. Each solver step is one matrix-vector product with $Q$ and a projection back onto the constraints $0 \le \alpha_i \le C$, $\sum_i y_i \alpha_i = 0$; the projection finds its Lagrange multiplier by testing 33 candidates at once and narrowing the bracket, a batched search instead of a loop. Thousands of cheap dense steps replace SMO's few clever sparse ones, and memory grows as $N^2$, so this version stops at some $10^4$ points where libsvm keeps going. Compare the dual objective and the predictions, not the multipliers one by one: many sets of $\alpha$ give almost the same objective.
cpuml.logreg.title: Logistic regression: autograd, and $C = 1/\lambda$
cpuml.logreg.text: Logistic regression is the simplest model trained by gradient descent: softmax probabilities, cross-entropy loss, an L2 penalty. scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` (multinomial, default solver `lbfgs` from SciPy) minimises $\tfrac12 \lVert W \rVert^2 + C \sum_n \mathrm{CE}_n$. Its `C` is the inverse of the usual regularisation strength, $C = 1/\lambda$ (here $C = {C}$), and the bias is not penalised.
cpuml.logreg.changes: Write the loss and let autograd write the gradient: `F.cross_entropy` fuses the softmax and the log, and `backward()` gives $\partial J / \partial W = X^\top (P - Y) + W / C$ (up to the factor $C$) without deriving it by hand. Match the regulariser exactly, `0.5 * (W**2).sum() + C * ce` with the bias left out of the penalty, or the coefficients will differ even where the accuracy agrees. The loss is divided by $CN$ before optimising (same minimiser, gradients of order one, so the tolerance means the same at every N). L-BFGS is the algorithm scikit-learn uses too; plain gradient descent, $W \leftarrow W - \eta \nabla J$, reaches the same point in many more steps, and mini-batches of it are how neural networks are trained.
cpuml.knn.title: k nearest neighbours: cdist and topk
cpuml.knn.text: The k-nearest-neighbour classifier gives a test point the majority label of its $k = {knn}$ closest training points. scikit-learn's `KNeighborsClassifier` chooses brute force or a tree (k-d or ball tree) from the shape of the data; at 64 or 784 dimensions trees do not help, and it computes the distances in chunks with BLAS.
cpuml.knn.changes: Three tensor lines: `torch.cdist` for every test-train distance (an (M, N) matrix, through a matrix product), `topk(k, largest=False)` for the k nearest, and `one_hot(...).sum(1).argmax(1)` for the vote. Ties go to the smallest label in both versions (`argmax` returns the first maximum). The (M, N) matrix is the cost: for very large N, process the queries in blocks. The same `cdist` and `topk` build the kNN graph of UMAP (card {umap}).
cpuml.kmeans.title: k-means: argmin and scatter-add
cpuml.kmeans.text: k-means splits the data into $k = {clusters}$ clusters by alternating two steps (Lloyd's algorithm): give every point to its nearest centre, then move every centre to the mean of its points. Both versions start from the same centres (the first {clusters} training points), run until no point changes cluster, and use scikit-learn's `algorithm="lloyd"` with `tol=0`.
cpuml.kmeans.changes: The assignment is `cdist` and `argmin` over all points at once; the update is a scatter-add: `index_add_` sums the points of every cluster in one call and `bincount` counts them. The loop over iterations stays (each step needs the previous centres); only the loops over points and clusters go. scikit-learn's k-means is already compiled, multi-threaded code (Cython with OpenMP), so on the CPU the tensor version has little to gain, and the GPU is where it pays.
cpuml.umap.title: UMAP: the full case study
cpuml.umap.text: UMAP (the umap-learn library, compiled loops through numba) is the largest migration on this site and has its own problem page. Its steps, each a batched tensor operation:
cpuml.umap.step.knn: **kNN graph.** Squared distances $\lVert x_i \rVert^2 + \lVert x_j \rVert^2 - 2\, x_i \cdot x_j$ in row blocks, then `topk`: exact neighbours, as in the kNN card.
cpuml.umap.step.sigma: **Bandwidths.** Every point's $\sigma_i$ solves $\sum_j e^{-(d_{ij} - \rho_i)/\sigma_i} = \log_2 k$; one bisection halves all $N$ brackets together (64 halvings) instead of looping over the points.
cpuml.umap.step.union: **Fuzzy union.** The memberships are scattered into $P$, then `P + P.T - P * P.T` gives symmetric edge weights in one line.
cpuml.umap.step.forces: **Edge-list forces.** Each epoch takes every active edge and 5 random negatives per edge, computes all attractive and repulsive forces at once and sums them per point with `index_add_` (a synchronous update, where umap-learn moves the points edge by edge). Autograd on the sampled loss gives the same step.
cpuml.umap.table: MNIST, 2500 digits, $k = 10$; wall time on the CPU, one thread
cpuml.umap.verdict: The tensor version matches umap-learn on every metric to within about 0.01 and takes a comparable time ({versions}; umap-learn's first call, with numba compilation, took {first} s). After the best rotation, reflection and scale, the two MNIST maps differ by a Procrustes disparity of {procrustes} (0 means the same shape). Limits: dense $N \times N$ matrices and a dense eigensolver keep this version below about $10^4$ points, and layouts are compared by metrics, never by coordinates.
cpuml.cuml.title: RAPIDS cuML: scikit-learn on the GPU, ready-made
cpuml.cuml.text: cuML, part of NVIDIA's RAPIDS libraries (now under the name CUDA-X Data Science), is a GPU machine-learning library with scikit-learn's interface: more than 50 algorithms, among them PCA, TruncatedSVD, k-means, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, linear and logistic regression, SVC and LinearSVC, k nearest neighbours, random forests, t-SNE and UMAP. Its `cuml.accel` mode runs an unchanged scikit-learn, umap-learn or hdbscan script on the GPU and falls back to the CPU for anything it cannot accelerate.
cpuml.cuml.codeTitle: cuML: zero code change, or explicit imports
cpuml.cuml.req: **Requirements.** Linux, or Windows 11 through WSL2 (no native Windows), and an NVIDIA GPU of the Volta generation or newer (compute capability 7.0+). Pascal support was removed in RAPIDS 24.02, so this project's GTX 1080 Ti cannot run it. Some options fall back to the CPU, for example `SVC` with more than two classes, `probability=True` or a precomputed kernel; the compatibility page lists them.
cpuml.cuml.useCuml: you already have scikit-learn or umap-learn code and a supported GPU (try `python -m cuml.accel` first: it costs one command); you need a mature implementation of an algorithm that is hard to write well (HDBSCAN, random forests, approximate nearest neighbours, sparse inputs); or you want scikit-learn's interface and behaviour, tested at scale.
cpuml.cuml.useTensor: the model must sit inside a PyTorch pipeline (gradients through it, a learned feature extractor before it, a custom loss after it); you need to batch many small problems at once, or change the objective; your platform has no cuML (native Windows, macOS with MPS, AMD or Intel GPUs, older NVIDIA GPUs); or you want to understand and test every step, as on this page.
