cpuml.bench.title: How it was measured
cpuml.machine: Tensor versions: {cpu}, {threads} threads{gpu}, PyTorch {torch}, float32, {date}; warm-up call, then the median of repeated calls, the whole set measured {passes} times. GPU timings are bracketed by `torch.cuda.synchronize()` and exclude copies to the device.
cpuml.skMachine: scikit-learn {sklearn} (NumPy {numpy}, SciPy {scipy}, BLAS: {blas}) ran in a throwaway environment (`pixi exec`, not a project dependency) on the same machine and the same data, {date}, with the same timing protocol. Each speed-up is the median scikit-learn time over the median tensor time.
cpuml.load: The machine was not idle: system CPU use was {lo}–{hi} % around the runs, which slows the CPU numbers of both sides; read absolute times with care.
cpuml.caveat: Times include the whole fit (and the prediction, for kNN); the timing data are synthetic (Gaussian blobs, or a low-rank matrix for PCA), float32, of the size shown. The numbers depend on the processor, the BLAS build, the GPU and what else is running. Reproduce them with:
cpuml.pca.result: **Result.** Same decomposition: the explained variance ratios agree to within 0.0000001 on the CPU and within $6 \times 10^{-6}$ on the GPU (float32), and the first 10 components are parallel up to sign ($|\cos| > 0.9999$). Speed: on the CPU both versions end in LAPACK, so the times are close (×1.1 to ×1.7, inside the spread); the GPU pulls ahead as N grows (×6.6 at 200 000 rows).
cpuml.linsvm.result: **Result.** Same model: equal test accuracy (86.8 %), identical predictions, the objective equal to 6 significant figures and the coefficients within 0.1 %. Speed: liblinear slows down as N grows (8 s at 100 000 points and ten classes), while L-BFGS on the batched (D+1, 10) matrix stays under a second on the CPU (×9) and reaches ×30 on the GPU. At 2000 points the GPU loses (×0.27): each L-BFGS step is a few small kernels and a synchronisation.
cpuml.ksvm.result: **Result.** Same solution: equal test accuracy (95.2 %), identical predictions, and the dual objective equal to 3 parts in a million (765 support vectors against libsvm's 763, a difference at the solvers' tolerance). Speed: here scikit-learn clearly wins, 6 to 10 times faster than the CPU tensor version, and even the GPU stays behind at 5000 points (×0.26). SMO touches only the few multipliers that matter and caches kernel rows; the dense method pays for the whole $N \times N$ matrix at every step. The tensor version earns its place when the kernel matrix is needed anyway or many SVMs are batched together; for one kernel SVM, keep libsvm (or cuML's GPU SVC).
cpuml.logreg.result: **Result.** Same model: the objective equal to 7 significant figures, the coefficients within 0.06 %, and 499 of the 500 test predictions equal (one digit on the decision boundary: accuracy 87.6 % against 87.8 %). Speed: at 2000 points SciPy's L-BFGS is faster (×0.65 against the CPU, ×0.15 against the GPU); from 20 000 points the tensor version wins, ×1.6 on the CPU and ×5.7 on the GPU at 100 000.
cpuml.knn.result: **Result.** Same predictions on all 500 test digits (89.8 % accuracy). Speed: the GPU wins at every size (×6 to ×11). On the CPU, scikit-learn's chunked brute force beats `cdist` and `topk` beyond a few thousand points (×0.6 to ×0.7): it never holds the whole distance matrix and selects the neighbours in compiled code.
cpuml.kmeans.result: **Result.** Same clustering: identical labels for all 2000 digits and the same inertia to 12 digits. Speed: scikit-learn's compiled k-means is 2 to 7 times faster than the CPU tensor version, and the GPU catches up only at 200 000 points (×1.6). A clear case where the migration buys portability and batching, not CPU speed.
cpuml.bench.observe: **Summary.** Every tensor version reproduces scikit-learn's result (same accuracy, objective to 6 or more significant figures, the same predictions), so each migration is correct. Speed depends on the case. Tensors win where scikit-learn's solver scales badly (LinearSVC: ×9 on the CPU at 100 000 points) and on the GPU at large N (PCA, linear models, kNN: ×6 to ×30). scikit-learn wins where it uses a smarter algorithm (SMO for kernel SVMs) or tight compiled loops (k-means, and kNN on the CPU), and on small data, where a GPU spends its time launching kernels. The GPU here is a 2017 GTX 1080 Ti; a newer one moves the balance further towards tensors at large N.
cpuml.anim.title: Animation: the algorithm as tensor operations (toy data)
cpuml.anim.codeTitle: The tensor code, line by line
cpuml.anim.pca.caption: Eight points in two dimensions stand in for the (N, D) data matrix. Centring is one broadcast subtraction, the SVD of the centred matrix gives the principal axes (rows of `Vh`, drawn as arrows two standard deviations long) and the singular values `S`, and the squared singular values give the explained variance ratio. Left: the points, $x_1$ and $x_2$ in arbitrary units (a.u.); the amber cross is the mean.
cpuml.anim.pca.s0: `X.mean(dim=0)`: average over the rows (dim 0), so the (8, 2) data become one (2,) mean vector, the amber cross.
cpuml.anim.pca.s1: `X - X.mean(dim=0)`: broadcasting stretches the (2,) mean over all 8 rows and subtracts it, so the whole cloud slides to the origin in one operation. The result `Xc` is still (8, 2).
cpuml.anim.pca.s2: `torch.linalg.svd(Xc)`: $X_c = U \, \mathrm{diag}(S) \, V_h$. The rows of `Vh` (2, 2) are the principal axes (blue: first, violet: second); `S` (2,) says how far the data spread along each.
cpuml.anim.pca.s3: `S**2 / (N - 1)` is the variance along each axis; divided by its sum it is the explained variance ratio `evr`: the first axis holds 94 % of the variance. Projecting on it (dashed line) keeps $k$ coordinates per point instead of $D$.
cpuml.anim.pca.code0: `Xc = X - X.mean(dim=0)`: the column means (D,) are subtracted from every row of the (N, D) matrix by broadcasting; PCA works on centred data.
cpuml.anim.pca.code1: `torch.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)`: the thin SVD, $X_c = U \, \mathrm{diag}(S) \, V_h$. The rows of `Vh` are the principal axes, sorted by decreasing `S`.
cpuml.anim.pca.code2: `var = S**2 / (X.shape[0] - 1)`: the variance of the data along each axis (the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, without ever forming that matrix).
cpuml.anim.pca.code3: `return Vh[:k], var[:k] / var.sum()`: the first $k$ axes, shape (k, D), like scikit-learn's `components_`, and their share of the total variance, like `explained_variance_ratio_`.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.caption: Four points with two features and three classes stand in for the MNIST data. All three one-vs-rest SVMs live in the columns of one weight matrix `W` (D+1, K), so one matrix product scores every point for every class and one loss trains them together. Colours: blue for positive values, amber for negative; in `hinge`, green cells are points already beyond the margin (zero loss).
cpuml.anim.linsvm.s0: `torch.cat` appends a column of ones: `Xb` (4, 3). Its row of `W` acts as the bias, penalised like the other weights, as in liblinear.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.s1: `y[:, None] == torch.arange(K)` compares the (4, 1) labels with the (3,) classes by broadcasting: a (4, 3) table, turned into $+1$ for the own class and $-1$ for the rest.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.s2: `Xb @ W`: (4, 3) @ (3, 3) gives the (4, 3) scores, row by row; entry $(n, k)$ is the score of point $n$ in the SVM of class $k$.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.s3: `(1 - Y * (Xb @ W)).clamp(min=0)`: the hinge, element by element. Zero (green) where the point is on its side with a margin of at least 1; positive (amber) where it is inside the margin or on the wrong side.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.s4: The loss is one number, $\tfrac12 \lVert W \rVert_F^2 + C \sum h_{nk}^2$; `loss.backward()` fills `W.grad` (3, 3), one gradient column per SVM, with no formula derived by hand.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.s5: `torch.optim.LBFGS` repeats loss and gradient until the gradient vanishes: `W*` minimises all three SVMs at once, the loss has dropped and `W.grad` is zero.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.code0: `Xb = torch.cat([X, torch.ones_like(X[:, :1])], dim=1)`: a column of ones, so the last row of `W` is a bias that the penalty treats like a weight (liblinear's convention).
cpuml.anim.linsvm.code1: `Y = 2.0 * (y[:, None] == torch.arange(N_CLASSES, device=X.device)) - 1`: the labels as an (N, K) table of $\pm 1$, one column per one-vs-rest problem.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.code2: `W = torch.zeros(..., requires_grad=True)` and `torch.optim.LBFGS([W], ...)`: one (D+1, K) parameter for all K SVMs. `requires_grad` lets autograd compute its gradient; the strong Wolfe line search keeps L-BFGS stable.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.code3: `objective()` computes `hinge = (1 - Y * (Xb @ W)).clamp(min=0)` and the loss, divides it by `C * len(X)` (same minimiser, gradients of order one) and calls `loss.backward()`; L-BFGS calls it as often as it needs.
cpuml.anim.linsvm.code4: `opt.step(objective)` runs the optimiser to convergence; `W.detach()` returns the weights without the autograd graph, shape (D+1, K), like scikit-learn's `coef_` and `intercept_` stacked.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.caption: Five points with two features and labels $y = \pm 1$ (blue circles $+1$, amber squares $-1$). The kernel matrix is built by broadcasting; then the dual is maximised by projected gradient steps, each one matrix-vector product with $Q$ followed by a projection onto $0 \le \alpha_i \le C$, $\sum_i y_i \alpha_i = 0$. Middle: the points, $x_1$ and $x_2$ in a.u. Right: the multiplier $\alpha_i$ (a.u.) of each point $i$, between 0 and $C = 1$ (red dashed line).
cpuml.anim.ksvm.s0: `sq = (X**2).sum(dim=1)` gives the squared norms (5,), and `X @ X.T` all dot products (5, 5) in one matrix product.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.s1: `sq[:, None] + sq[None, :] - 2 * X @ X.T`: a (5, 1) column plus a (1, 5) row broadcast to (5, 5), every squared distance $\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2$ without a loop.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.s2: `torch.exp(-gamma * D2)`: the RBF kernel, element by element: 1 on the diagonal, near 0 for distant pairs. $\gamma$ is scikit-learn's `gamma="scale"`.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.s3: `K * (y[:, None] * y[None, :])`: the outer product of the labels (broadcasting again) flips the sign of pairs from different classes, $Q_{ij} = y_i y_j K_{ij}$.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.s4: Each iteration: the gradient of the dual is `1 - Q @ z`, one (5, 5) @ (5,) product; a step of $1/L$, then `project` back into the box and onto the plane. The dual objective rises and the multipliers settle; point 0 ends at $\alpha_0 = 0$.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.s5: Converged. Points with $\alpha_i > 0$ (green rings) are the support vectors; point 4, at $\alpha_4 = C$, lies inside the margin. The decision values are `K @ (a * y)`, and $b$ comes from the support vectors with $0 < \alpha_i < C$.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.code0: `sq` and the `K = torch.exp(...)` line: the whole (N, N) RBF kernel matrix by broadcasting; `clamp(min=0)` removes tiny negative distances left by rounding.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.code1: `Q = K * (y[:, None] * y[None, :])`: the matrix of the dual problem, $Q_{ij} = y_i y_j K_{ij}$.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.code2: The power iteration (`v = Q @ v`, normalised, 30 times) estimates the largest eigenvalue `L` of $Q$; $1/L$ is a step size that cannot overshoot.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.code3: The main loop is FISTA, accelerated projected gradient ascent: a gradient step from `z`, `project` back onto the constraints, and a momentum step that mixes the new and the previous `a`. Every 50 iterations it stops if the dual objective no longer rises.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.code4: `project` finds the closest feasible point $\alpha = \mathrm{clip}(v - \mu y, 0, C)$: it evaluates 33 candidate values of $\mu$ at once, keeps the interval where $\sum_i y_i \alpha_i$ crosses zero, and repeats this 5 times.
cpuml.anim.ksvm.code5: `f = K @ (a * y)` gives the decision values; the bias `b` averages $y_i - f_i$ over the margin support vectors ($0 < \alpha_i < C$).
cpuml.anim.logreg.caption: Four points with two features and three classes; one training step as tensors. A matrix product and a broadcast bias give the scores, softmax turns each row into probabilities, and the gradient is again one matrix product, $X^\top (P - Y)$. The card's code uses L-BFGS, which takes better steps than the plain step shown, but from this same gradient. Colours: blue for positive values, amber for negative.
cpuml.anim.logreg.s0: `X @ W`: (4, 2) @ (2, 3) gives one score per point and class, row by row.
cpuml.anim.logreg.s1: `+ b`: the (3,) bias is broadcast over the 4 rows, giving the logits `Z` (4, 3).
cpuml.anim.logreg.s2: `softmax(Z, dim=1)` exponentiates and normalises each row, so every row of `P` is a probability distribution over the 3 classes (it sums to 1).
cpuml.anim.logreg.s3: `P - Y`, with `Y` the one-hot labels: positive where the model gives probability to a wrong class, negative for the true class.
cpuml.anim.logreg.s4: `loss.backward()` computes `W.grad` $= X^\top (P - Y) + W / C$, shape (2, 3) like `W`: one matrix product, no derivative written by hand.
cpuml.anim.logreg.s5: A step against the gradient lowers the loss $J / C$; L-BFGS repeats this, with step sizes from its curvature estimate, until the gradient vanishes.
cpuml.anim.logreg.code0: `W` (D, K) and `b` (K,) start at zero with `requires_grad=True`, so autograd tracks them; the bias is a separate tensor because scikit-learn does not penalise it.
cpuml.anim.logreg.code1: `cross_entropy(X @ W + b, y, reduction="sum")`: logits, softmax and the negative log-probability of the true class in one numerically stable call, summed over the points.
cpuml.anim.logreg.code2: `loss = (0.5 * (W**2).sum() + C * ce) / (C * len(X))`: exactly scikit-learn's objective (the L2 penalty on `W` only, $C = 1/\lambda$), divided by a constant that does not move the minimiser.
cpuml.anim.logreg.code3: `loss.backward()` writes the gradients into `W.grad` and `b.grad`; `opt.step(objective)` (L-BFGS) uses them until convergence, and `torch.cat([W, b[None]])` returns the (D+1, K) result stacked like scikit-learn's.
cpuml.anim.knn.caption: Eight training points of three classes (coloured dots) and three queries $q_m$ (diamonds), with $k = 3$. The whole classifier is three tensor calls: a distance matrix, a top-k selection along each row and a vote. Left: the points, $x_1$ and $x_2$ in a.u.; the amber lines join each query to its $k$ nearest neighbours.
cpuml.anim.knn.s0: `torch.cdist(Xte, Xtr)`: every query-to-training distance at once, a (3, 8) matrix, one row per query (darker is farther).
cpuml.anim.knn.s1: `topk(k, largest=False)`: along each row, the indices of the $k$ smallest distances, `idx` (3, 3) (amber cells).
cpuml.anim.knn.s2: `ytr[idx]` looks up the labels of the neighbours (3, 3); `one_hot(..., K).sum(dim=1)` counts them per class: `votes` (3, 3).
cpuml.anim.knn.s3: `votes.argmax(dim=1)`: the class with the most votes is the prediction (3,), and each query takes its colour. Ties would go to the smallest label, as in scikit-learn.
cpuml.anim.knn.code0: `d = torch.cdist(Xte, Xtr)`: the (M, N) distances between M test and N training points, computed through a matrix product.
cpuml.anim.knn.code1: `idx = d.topk(k, largest=False).indices`: the positions of the k nearest training points of every test point, (M, k); no full sort is needed.
cpuml.anim.knn.code2: `one_hot(ytr[idx], N_CLASSES).sum(dim=1)`: gather the neighbours' labels (M, k), turn each into a one-hot row and add them up: votes per class (M, K).
cpuml.anim.knn.code3: `votes.argmax(dim=1)`: the winning class of each test point. `argmax` returns the first maximum, so ties go to the smallest label, as in scikit-learn.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.caption: Nine points and $k = 3$ clusters; the centres (crosses) start at the first three points, as in the benchmark. Each Lloyd iteration is two tensor steps: give every point to its nearest centre (`cdist`, `argmin`), then move every centre to the mean of its points (`index_add_`, `bincount`). It stops when no label changes. Left: $x_1$ and $x_2$ in a.u.; the colours are the clusters.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.s0: `torch.cdist(X, centers)`: the (9, 3) distances from every point to every centre (darker is farther).
cpuml.anim.kmeans.s1: `argmin(dim=1)`: the nearest centre of each point, `labels` (9,); the points take their cluster's colour.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.s2: `index_add_(0, labels, X)` adds each point's row into the row of its cluster, `sums` (3, 2), in one call; `bincount(labels)` counts the points per cluster (3,).
cpuml.anim.kmeans.s3: `sums / counts[:, None]`: (3, 2) divided by (3, 1), broadcast. The new centres are the cluster means, and the crosses move.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.s4: After the next assignment `torch.equal(new, labels)` is true: no point changed cluster, so the algorithm has converged.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.code0: `labels = torch.cdist(X, centers).argmin(dim=1)`: the first assignment (N,), from the starting centres.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.code1: `sums = torch.zeros_like(centers).index_add_(0, labels, X)`: a scatter-add; row `labels[n]` of the (k, D) result receives row `n` of `X`, for every n at once.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.code2: `counts = torch.bincount(labels, minlength=len(centers)).clamp(min=1)`: points per cluster, at least 1 so that an empty cluster does not divide by zero; `centers = sums / counts[:, None]` broadcasts the division over the D columns.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.code3: `new = torch.cdist(X, centers).argmin(dim=1)`: reassign every point to the moved centres.
cpuml.anim.kmeans.code4: `if torch.equal(new, labels): break`: stop as soon as no label changes (scikit-learn's criterion with `tol=0`). The `while` loop over iterations stays, because each step needs the previous centres.
cpuml.plot.title: How to read the table and the chart
cpuml.plot.common: **Chart.** One row per size N, from small to large. Every bar starts at the thin vertical line, 1× (as fast as scikit-learn); its length is the speed-up $t_{\mathrm{sklearn}} / t_{\mathrm{tensor}}$, dimensionless, on a log scale. To the right the tensor code is faster, to the left scikit-learn is (the number turns amber). Blue: the tensor code on the CPU; green: the same code on the GPU. The black |–| spans the least to the most favourable timing pass, so a bar whose error bar crosses 1× is a tie. Under each N: scikit-learn's own time, for scale.
cpuml.plot.pca: **Table** (MNIST, {k} components of the 784 pixel features). The first two rows are explained variance ratios (fractions of the total variance, dimensionless) and should be equal in every column. Then the largest difference of any ratio from scikit-learn (near 0 is good) and the smallest $|\cos|$ between matching components (near 1 is good; components are compared up to sign), and the time. The chart's data are synthetic: low-rank, 128 features; N is the number of rows of the data matrix.
cpuml.plot.linsvm: **Table** (MNIST, 10 digits, one-vs-rest). Test accuracy (share of test digits classified correctly) and the objective value $J$ (dimensionless) should agree in every column; then the share of test predictions equal to scikit-learn's (100 % is perfect) and the largest coefficient difference relative to the largest coefficient (near 0 is good). The chart's data are synthetic Gaussian blobs with 64 features and 10 classes; N is the number of training points.
cpuml.plot.ksvm: **Table** (MNIST, even against odd digits). Equal test accuracy and equal predictions mean the same classifier; the dual objective (dimensionless, higher is better) shows how close each solver gets to the optimum, and the number of support vectors (points with $\alpha_i > 0$) may differ by a few at the solvers' tolerance. The chart's data are synthetic blobs with 32 features and two classes; N is the number of training points. The kernel matrix has $N^2$ entries, so the sizes stop at 5000.
cpuml.plot.logreg: **Table** (MNIST, 10 digits). Test accuracy, the objective value (dimensionless, one formula for both, so equal values mean the same minimum), the share of predictions equal to scikit-learn's and the largest relative coefficient difference (near 0 is good). The chart's data are synthetic blobs with 64 features and 10 classes; N is the number of training points.
cpuml.plot.knn: **Table** (MNIST, $k = {knn}$). kNN has no training objective, so agreement means the test accuracy and the share of predictions equal to scikit-learn's (100 % means the same neighbours were found). The chart's data are synthetic blobs with 64 features; N is the number of training points, searched by 1000 queries each time, and the time includes the prediction.
cpuml.plot.kmeans: **Table** (MNIST training digits, $k = {clusters}$). The inertia (sum of squared distances to the nearest centre, in squared feature units) and the share of labels equal to scikit-learn's; equal inertia to many digits and 100 % equal labels mean the same clustering. The chart's data are synthetic blobs with 32 features and 10 clusters; N is the number of points clustered.
feynman.title: The Feynman technique: explain it simply, find the gaps, repeat
feynman.intro: The other tabs on this site are written "the Feynman way". This tab explains the way itself: what the four steps are, where they really come from, how Richard Feynman explained things, and how to use the steps on a piece of tensor maths.
feynman.note: **A word on names and quotes.** Feynman never wrote down a "Feynman technique". The four steps below are a later summary of his habits, popularised on blogs and in books from about 2011. Quotes on this page are marked **verbatim** when the original wording survives in writing, and **reported** when it reaches us through someone else's account.
feynman.steps.title: The four steps
feynman.steps.plain: Pick something you want to understand and try to teach it, on paper, to someone who has never heard of it. Wherever your explanation stalls, or needs a word you cannot explain, you have found the edge of your understanding. Go back to the source, fill the hole, and try again in simpler words.
feynman.steps.analogy: It is like checking a bridge by walking across it. Reading about a subject is looking at the bridge from the bank: it seems solid. Explaining it is walking over it plank by plank, and the missing planks show themselves under your feet.
feynman.steps.precise: The four steps as they are usually given: **(1)** pick a concept and write down what you already know about it; **(2)** explain it in plain words, as if to a 12-year-old or a newcomer; **(3)** find the gaps, the places where the explanation breaks or leans on jargon, and go back to the source material; **(4)** simplify and use analogies, then repeat from step 2 until the explanation runs from start to end without a gap.
feynman.steps.example: Try "why is the sky blue?". Step 2 often gives "because the air scatters blue light". Step 3 asks: why blue more than red? That is the gap. The source says that scattering by molecules much smaller than the wavelength grows like $1/\lambda^4$, so blue light (about 450 nm) is scattered about $(700/450)^4 \approx 6$ times more than red light (about 700 nm). Step 4: "tiny air molecules shake best at short wavelengths, so they throw blue light around the sky far more than red".
feynman.step1.title: Pick and write
feynman.step1.text: Name the concept at the top of a blank page. Write down everything you already know, without looking anything up.
feynman.step2.title: Explain it simply
feynman.step2.text: Explain it in plain words to an imagined newcomer, say a curious 12-year-old. No jargon you have not explained.
feynman.step3.title: Find the gaps
feynman.step3.text: Mark every place where you got stuck, waved your hands or reached for jargon. Go back to the source for exactly those points.
feynman.step4.title: Simplify and repeat
feynman.step4.text: Rewrite with simpler words and an analogy. Read it aloud. Repeat from step 2 until nothing breaks.
feynman.cycle: Repeat steps 2 to 4 until the explanation has no gaps
feynman.steps.origin: **Who named it?** The phrase "Feynman technique" and the four-step recipe are not in Feynman's books or lectures. An early, dated use is Scott Young's blog post "Learn faster with the Feynman technique" (September 2011); Cal Newport and many others then wrote about it. The recipe is a fair summary of how Feynman worked, as the next section shows, but it is a modern synthesis, not his method in his own words.
feynman.roots.title: What Feynman actually said and did
feynman.roots.intro: Four things Feynman wrote, said or did are the real roots of the technique. Each card says how sure we can be of the wording; the original English is shown under the text.
feynman.roots.notebook.title: A notebook of things he did not know
feynman.roots.notebook.text: As a young physicist he opened a fresh notebook, titled it "Notebook of things I don't know about" and worked through physics, reorganising what he knew. That is steps 1 and 3 at once: write down what you know, and hunt for what you do not.
feynman.roots.notebook.how: Reported: told by his biographer James Gleick (Genius, 1992) and quoted by Cal Newport (2015). The exact title may differ between accounts.
feynman.roots.create.title: "What I cannot create, I do not understand"
feynman.roots.create.text: This sentence was on his blackboard at Caltech when he died in February 1988. For him, understanding meant being able to rebuild a result yourself from the beginning, not just to recognise it when you see it.
feynman.roots.create.how: Verbatim: in chalk on his blackboard; the Caltech Archives keep a photograph of the board as he left it (1988).
feynman.roots.freshman.title: The freshman lecture test
feynman.roots.freshman.text: His colleague David Goodstein once asked him why spin-1/2 particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics. Feynman said he would prepare a freshman lecture on it. A few days later he came back and admitted that he could not: he could not bring it down to the level of first-year students, which meant, he said, that physicists did not really understand it. Failing step 2 told him something about physics, not about the students.
feynman.roots.freshman.how: Reported: Feynman's words as remembered by Goodstein (Physics Today, 1989). The popular line about explaining things "to a first-year student" is a paraphrase of this story, not a Feynman quote.
feynman.roots.lectures.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics
feynman.roots.lectures.text: From 1961 to 1963 he taught the introductory physics course at Caltech, building physics up from scratch for first- and second-year students. The lectures became three books, which Caltech now publishes free to read online, so you can watch him build an explanation step by step.
feynman.roots.lectures.how: Primary source: the lectures themselves, free online at feynmanlectures.caltech.edu.
feynman.life.title: Feynman's own story, as an explainer
feynman.life.intro: Only the parts of his life that show how he explained things. Every fact has a source at the end of the section.
feynman.life.losalamos.title: Los Alamos: explaining the why
feynman.life.losalamos.text: On the Manhattan Project he was a group leader in Hans Bethe's Theoretical Division and helped set up calculations on IBM punched-card machines. The young operators had not been told what the numbers were for. Once he was allowed to explain the project to them, they found their own ways to work faster: by his account, three problems in nine months became nine problems in three months. At Oak Ridge he explained neutrons and safety to the plant engineers, who then formed their own groups to do the safety calculations.
feynman.life.diagrams.title: Pictures instead of pages of algebra
feynman.life.diagrams.text: In quantum electrodynamics (QED), the theory of light and electrons, he drew each term of a calculation as a small picture of particles meeting and exchanging a photon. These Feynman diagrams, published in 1949, turned pages of algebra into drawings that physicists could count and check. The Penrose diagrams on the Tensor maths tab play the same trick for tensors.
feynman.life.diagrams.link: Try it on this site: the problem $e^+e^- \to \mu^+\mu^-$, one Feynman diagram computed with tensors
feynman.life.nobel.title: The Nobel Prize
feynman.life.nobel.text: He shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Sin-Itiro Tomonaga and Julian Schwinger "for their fundamental work in quantum electrodynamics". Three people reached the same theory by different routes; Feynman's route was the pictorial one.
feynman.life.challenger.title: A glass of ice water
feynman.life.challenger.text: After the Space Shuttle Challenger broke up on 28 January 1986, he served on the Rogers Commission. At a televised hearing he squeezed a piece of the booster's O-ring rubber in a small clamp, put it in a glass of ice water and showed that, when cold, it did not spring back. One cheap demonstration said what pages of testimony had not. His appendix to the report ends: "For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled." Unfortunately, for all the brilliance of Feynman's presentation, seventeen years later NASA repeated the very same mistakes with Columbia in a strikingly similar and heartbreaking way.

feynman.site.title: How this site uses the technique
feynman.site.intro: The explanations on this site are built from the same four steps. Here is where to see each one at work.
feynman.site.maths.title: Steps 2 and 4: Picture it, Precisely, Tiny example
feynman.site.maths.text: Each section of the Tensor maths tab goes in the same order: in plain words (step 2), a picture from everyday life (the analogy of step 4), then the precise statement and a tiny example you can check by hand. If the plain words and the precise statement disagree, one of them has a gap.
feynman.site.ladder.title: Step 1 on paper: the formulation ladder
feynman.site.ladder.text: The From law to simulation tab climbs from a physical picture to the vector form of the law, then to the index form, then to code. Each rung says the same idea in a stricter language, and a missing index or a wrong sign shows up as you climb.
feynman.site.tdd.title: Step 3 made automatic: write the test first
feynman.site.tdd.text: Test-driven development writes the check before the code: a small-angle period, conserved energy, a known answer. A failing test is a gap found by the computer instead of by you, and it tells you exactly where to go back to the source.
feynman.example.title: Worked example: contraction and einsum
feynman.example.intro: The four steps applied to one idea used all over this site: the tensor contraction, written in code as `einsum`.
feynman.example.s1.title: Step 1: what I already know
feynman.example.s1.text: `einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)` is a matrix product. The letters are indices. The string says which indices go in and which come out. It also does dot products, traces and batches of products.
feynman.example.s2.title: Step 2: a first attempt in plain words
feynman.example.s2.text: "You give every side of every array a letter, and einsum multiplies the arrays together and hands back the sides you asked for."
feynman.example.s3.title: Step 3: the gap
feynman.example.s3.text: "Multiplies them together" hides the real question: **what happens to the repeated index?** In `ij,jk->ik` the letter `j` appears in both inputs but not in the output. Back to the source (Einstein's rule and the einsum documentation): an index that appears in the inputs but not in the output is **summed over**; an index kept in the output is free and is not summed. So `i,j->ij` (an outer product) sums nothing, and `ii->` (a trace) sums the diagonal.
feynman.example.s4.title: Step 4: simpler, with an analogy
feynman.example.s4.text: "Each letter is a label on one side of a box of numbers. Two boxes that share a label are zipped together along that side: the numbers that meet are multiplied, the products are added up, and the shared side disappears. Labels that only one box has stay on the outside of the result." Like a till receipt: for each customer, multiply the quantity of each product by its price and add over the products. The product names are gone from the bottom line; one total per customer remains.
feynman.example.check: **Check by hand.** Two customers, two products: quantities $Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, prices $p = (3, 5)$. `einsum("ij,j->i", Q, p)` gives $(2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 5,\ 0 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 5) = (11, 15)$: the product index $j$ is summed and gone, the customer index $i$ stays.
feynman.pform.title: Two ways to write p
feynman.pform.help: In index form, $p_j$ is just two numbers labelled by j, $p_1 = 3$ and $p_2 = 5$: it has no row or column, so writing $p = (3, 5)$ on one line is fine. In matrix form, the product $Q\,p$ needs p as a column, so that each row of Q meets it number by number. The picture above draws p as that column. Both give $(11, 15)$.
feynman.pitfalls.title: Common pitfalls and a self-check
feynman.pitfalls.intro: The technique is simple, which makes it easy to do badly. Three common ways it goes wrong:
feynman.pitfalls.p1: **Simplifying until it is wrong.** "A tensor is just a matrix with more dimensions" is simple and, for physics, misleading (see the misconceptions at the end of the Tensor maths tab). Simple must still be true: drop detail, never correctness, and say what you left out.
feynman.pitfalls.p2: **Analogies that break.** Every analogy fails somewhere. The zip analogy for einsum says nothing about how much a contraction costs, or in which order several should be done. Use an analogy to get started, then say where it stops working.
feynman.pitfalls.p3: **Skipping step 3.** A fluent explanation to yourself proves little. In his 1974 Caltech commencement address Feynman put it this way (verbatim): the first principle is that "you must not fool yourself", and "you are the easiest person to fool". Gaps have to be hunted: by a real listener, a test, or a tiny example worked by hand.
feynman.check.title: Self-check: can you tick every box?
feynman.check.c1: I can explain it without any word I could not define for a newcomer.
feynman.check.c2: I can give one tiny example and work it out by hand.
feynman.check.c3: I can say where my analogy stops working.
feynman.check.c4: I went back to the source for every point where I got stuck.
feynman.check.c5: Someone else, or a test, has checked my explanation, not only me.
feynman.check.c6: I can rebuild the result from the beginning, not just recognise it.
feynman.check.done: Every box ticked. Now explain it to someone else and see what they ask.

reading.title: Further reading: the books behind this site
reading.intro: Eighteen books for going further, in four groups. Start with the ones marked **★ Top pick**. Each card also links to the tab of this site that the book takes deeper.
reading.disclosure: As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.
reading.note: All Amazon links on this page are affiliate links.
reading.book.fleisch.why: The gentlest start: vectors, covariant and contravariant components and the metric, in plain words with a picture for every idea.
reading.book.grinfeld.why: Index notation done carefully, from the metric tensor and Christoffel symbols to the covariant derivative, with every step written out.
reading.book.strang.why: Linear algebra as deep learning uses it: matrix factorisations, low rank, and the optimisation behind training.
reading.book.penrose.why: A tour of the mathematics of physics by the inventor of the diagram notation for tensors used on the maths tab.
reading.book.lectures.why: Feynman's own introductory course at Caltech, still the clearest account of mechanics, electromagnetism and quantum physics.
reading.book.qed.why: Four public lectures that explain quantum electrodynamics with arrows instead of equations: the Feynman technique at its best.
reading.book.surely.why: Feynman's stories, from safe-cracking at Los Alamos to drumming in Brazil, and a good picture of how he learned anything new.
reading.book.genius.why: The standard biography: how Feynman's way of thinking took shape, and how his diagrams changed physics.
reading.book.schutz.why: A clear first course in Einstein's theory, built on tensors from the start; this edition adds gravitational waves.
reading.book.pmpp.why: The standard textbook on GPU programming in CUDA: threads, the memory hierarchy, tiling and the patterns behind fast tensor code.
reading.book.udl.why: A modern, well illustrated deep learning textbook, from the maths of networks to transformers and diffusion models.
reading.book.hp.why: The reference on how processors and memory systems work, and where the roofline model comes from.
reading.book.pytorch.why: A practical guide to tensors in PyTorch, from the basics to training and applying real models.
reading.book.bishop.why: A thorough, self-contained deep learning textbook by the author of Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning.
reading.book.chipwar.why: How the microchip was invented, who makes it today, and why it became the world's most contested technology.
reading.book.pais.why: The definitive scientific biography of Einstein, by a physicist who knew him: how he learned tensor calculus with Grossmann and fought his way to the field equations, with the mathematics in full.
reading.book.witt.why: The story of Jensen Huang and Nvidia, from graphics cards to CUDA and the hardware behind modern AI.
reading.book.worlds.why: A memoir by the creator of ImageNet, the dataset that set off the deep learning boom in 2012.

maths.topo.takeaway: Which strings you tie first can make the job ten times shorter.
maths.topo.misconception: **“Changing the grouping makes no difference.”** Keeping matrix order fixed, regrouping preserves the exact mathematical result, but intermediate sizes and computational cost can change dramatically.
maths.roof.misconception: **"A faster GPU makes every kernel faster."** Only compute-bound ones. A memory-bound kernel runs at the speed of memory; more FLOP/s cannot help it, while fusion or better reuse of data can.
